reasoning: Both sets are rigorous, well-structured plans with frozen contracts, spine/wire/system phases and per-task context packets. Set A wins narrowly on how buildable and testable its first milestone is. M1 is backed by 27 synthetic known-answer golden cases (TC-01–TC-27) that the thicken tasks point to by number. It has one interface task for all three packages, so no interface task waits on another. Its architecture states the hard quant conventions outright: delisting and gap returns (AD-08), backtest timing and costs (AD-23), parallel analysis for the factor count (AD-12), the lockbox rule (AD-25), and the reference caveats fixed in AD-12, AD-15 and AD-16. It also covers every stage, PPO agents and the rented GPU included. Its biggest misses: it drops the yahooquery cross-check and your list of 10 delisted names entirely; CONSTRAINTS.md is cited but missing; the designed milestones carry no References lines; and the Membership invariant contradicts its own TC-18. Set B is strong on the user's research needs. It checks the 10 delisted names (CHECK-09), has a Yahoo cross-check (XCHK), runs known-answer gates before real data (SYNTH, FSYN), adds calibration features and power statements, spells out what each null-hypothesis-testing call receives, has the user approve a frontend-design direction first, and places references on milestones (RF-01 on M4 and M6, RF-02 and RF-03 on M8). But it drops PPO agents and the rented GPU from S4, uses yfinance where you asked for yahooquery, and has no golden cases at all for the data package in M1. Its three interface tasks run in parallel even though their imports depend on each other, several 'spine' tasks are labelled Kind: thicken, a server packet leaves nested message types and route paths undefined, and the 744-line spec is heavy for a solo learner.
